title: Moving integer division to floating-point is trivial
excerpt: Shows that floating point trunc(x/y) equals integer x/y provided the integers fit in the floating point format.
content_html:
Integer division q=(x/y) and remainder (of Euclidean division) r=(x%y) hardware operations are very sad on current hardware. Typically very long latency and poor throughput. In contrast floating-point division is pretty happy: shorter latency, higher throughput and often more execution units to perform the operation. So there are cases it could be interesting to move some integer div/mod operations to floating point. But it’s PITA right? Actually I think it’s easy. The math is pretty straightforward so if I’ve made a mistake I expect to find out rather soon.

My claim is: for two integers x & y (signed or unsigned) that fit in 53/24 bits for double/single precision respectively, with both promoted to floating point then:

// floating-point:
//   d is the same integer as integer divide    x / y
//   m is the same integer as integer remainder x % y
//   (in standard rounding mode: round-to-nearest, ties to even)

d = trunc(x/y);     // floor works for unsigned
m = -fma(d,y,-x);   // fma required

// NOTE: if only want 'd' and it's being converted to an
// integer then the truncate or floor operation is
// free in the float to integer conversion.


in standard rounding mode.

From here on I will only consider unsigned integers since it’s the harder case (signed have a smaller max magnitude) but recall that floating point effective stores a signed magnitude quantity.

Some practical points:

  • this works by setting rounding-mode to TOWARD_ZERO and then back once done but hitting control words is often very expensive
  • some hardware have division opcodes that allow choosing the rounding mode on some operations like division. Example AVX-512 has instrinsic: _mm_div_round_sd with example listed latency of 14 cycles.
  • converting int to float and back has a cost. (NOTE: the majority of x64 CPUs don’t have an op for unsigned to float and back. So this is an implemenation concern.)
  • obviously the floating point precision $p$ places the upper bound on integer width. If this works for $p$ then all smaller widths trivally work. Examples 32-bit integers in doubles ($p=53$) and 16-bit integers in singles ($p=24$). In this case it’s possible that there’s some “trickery” to side-step the int to float.
  • obviously the most promising case is for working in SIMD to amortize overhead.
  • for constant divisors your compiler should eliminate. for runtime known divisors that are going to be reused a small number of times there’s software solutions like libdivide.

Note that there are proven methods (SEE: Formally verified 32- and 64-bit integer division using double-precision floating-point arithmetic)

The standard rounding mode is: round-to-nearest (ties to even) and the first important observation is the ties part. A tie happens when the exact result of an operation is exactly at the midpoint between two floating point numbers. Floating point division (in our case of base-2 and same working precision) has zero midpoints (SEE: Midpoints and exact points of some algebraic functions in floating-point arithmetic section 6.1, corollary 1). Therefore there’s never a tie and only round-to-nearest portion applies.

Let’s look an example using a 4-bit precision floating point format with all possible configurations where the exact result is less than one but as close as possible to rounding up:

      |GRS            x = don't care
 .1111|0xx   .1111    (no rounding)
 .1111|100            tie case is impossible
 .1111|101  1.000     (round up)
 .1111|11x  1.000     (round up)


Prior to rounding the hardware computes three extra digits: guard bit (G), round bit (R) and sticky bit (S) but since the tie case is impossible we only need to know G. Therefore in any format where the exact result has $r$ bits for the fractional part then for rounding to the next integer to occur requires the fractional part to have at least $r+1$ leading ones. I’m claiming that this is impossible with legal inputs.


Since we only need to consider what happens with the fractional part let’s breakdown the exact result of $x/y$ into its integer $n$ and fractional parts:

\[\frac{x}{y} = n + \frac{a}{b}\]


(where $b=y$ just to be less of an eyesore) so obviously:

\[\frac{a}{b} \in \left[0,1\right)\]

Given a $p$ precision binary floating point format the division produces a $d$-bit integer leaving $r$-bits for the remainder:

\[\begin{align*} d & = \left \lfloor \log_2 \left(n \right)+1 \right \rfloor \\ r & = p-d \\ \end{align*}\]

For a $r$-bit fractional part we can define the lower and upper bound on it’s range of value for $b$:

\[\begin{align*} \func{b_l}{r} & = 2^r \\ \func{b_u}{r} & = 2^{r+1}-1 \end{align*}\]

At this point we’re pretty much done with $p$, $n$ and its derived $d$. We want to know the maximum fractional part possible for $r$-bits.

The closest value to $1$ we can create with the lower is:

\[\begin{align*} \frac{2^r-1}{2^r} = \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{1}{2^i} \end{align*}\]


Rewritten as the sum tells us that this is the smallest number that produces $r$ leading ones in it’s binary expansion.

Now repeating with the upper bound’s closest to $1$ value and compare to the smallest number with $r+1$ leading ones (the lower bound of $r+1$):

\[\begin{align*} \frac{2^{r+1}-2}{2^{r+1}-1} &< \frac{2^{r+1}-1}{2^{r+1}-0} \end{align*}\]


where the minus zero is to align the expressions and highlight the pattern. Anyway this inequality means that the upper bound is limited to having $r$ leading ones.

We can actually be specific about the binary expansion of bounds. The lower is $r$ ones and terminating. The upper’s exact value is purely cyclic with a period of $r+1$ with $r$ ones followed by one zero. Here’s a table for the first four:

$r$ lower binary expansion upper binary expansion
1 $\frac{1}{2}$ .1 $\frac{2}{3} $ .(10)
2 $\frac{3}{4}$ .11 $\frac{6}{7} $ .(110)
3 $\frac{7}{8}$ .111 $\frac{14}{15}$ .(1110)
4 $\frac{15}{16}$ .1111 $\frac{30}{31}$ .(11110)


But anyway the important part:


Let’s briefly tie the parts together by considering some divisors.

Dividing by:

  • $1$ is correct
  • $2$ only modifies the exponent and no rounding of any kind occurs.
  • $3$ which is $r=1$, the largest x % 3 value is $2$ so max fraction is $\frac{2}{3}$. Can’t round to next integer.
  • $\set{4,5,6,7}$ have $r=2$. The exact divisor doesn’t matter because they all start with .110x.

And so on all possible divisors.

content_html_zh:
整数除法 q=(x/y) 和余数（欧几里得除法） r=(x%y) 硬件运算在当前硬件上非常糟糕。 通常延迟很长，吞吐量很差。 相比之下，浮点除法非常令人满意：延迟更短，吞吐量更高，并且通常有更多的执行单元来执行操作。 因此，在某些情况下，将一些整数 div/mod 运算移至浮点可能会很有趣。 但这是 PITA 对吗？ 其实我觉得这很容易。 数学非常简单，所以如果我犯了一个错误，我希望很快就能发现。

我的主张是：对于两个整数 x 和 y（有符号或无符号），分别适合双精度/单精度的 53/24 位，然后两者都提升为浮点数：

// floating-point:
//   d is the same integer as integer divide    x / y
//   m is the same integer as integer remainder x % y
//   (in standard rounding mode: round-to-nearest, ties to even)

d = trunc(x/y);     // floor works for unsigned
m = -fma(d,y,-x);   // fma required

// NOTE: if only want 'd' and it's being converted to an
// integer then the truncate or floor operation is
// free in the float to integer conversion.

在标准舍入模式下。

从这里开始，我将只考虑无符号整数，因为它是更困难的情况（有符号的最大值较小），但请记住，浮点有效存储有符号的大小数量。

一些实用要点：

  • 这是通过将舍入模式设置为 TOWARD_ZERO 并在完成后返回来实现的，但命中控制字通常非常昂贵
  • 某些硬件具有除法操作码，允许在除法等某些操作上选择舍入模式。 示例 AVX-512 具有固有的：_mm_div_round_sd，示例列出的延迟为 14 个周期。
  • 将 int 转换为 float 并返回是有成本的。 （注意：大多数 x64 CPU 没有用于无符号浮点和返回的操作。 所以这是一个实施问题。）
  • 显然，浮点精度 $p$ 将上限置于整数宽度上。 如果这适用于 $p$，那么所有较小的宽度都可以正常工作。 示例 双精度数中的 32 位整数 ($p=53$) 和单精度数中的 16 位整数 ($p=24$)。 在这种情况下，可能存在一些“技巧”来回避 int 浮动。
  • 显然，最有希望的情况是使用 SIMD 来分摊开销。
  • 对于常量除数，您的编译器应该消除。 对于要重复使用少量次的运行时已知除数，有像 libdivide 这样的软件解决方案。

请注意，有经过验证的方法（参见：使用双精度浮点运算正式验证的 32 位和 64 位整数除法）

标准舍入模式是：舍入到最接近的值（连到偶数），第一个重要的观察结果是连线部分。 当运算的确切结果恰好位于两个浮点数之间的中点时，就会发生平局。 浮点除法（在我们的基数为 2 且工作精度相同的情况下）的中点为零（参见：浮点算术第 6.1 节，推论 1 中某些代数函数的中点和精确点）。 因此，永远不会有平局，只适用四舍五入到最接近的部分。

让我们看一个使用 4 位精度浮点格式以及所有可能配置的示例，其中精确结果小于 1，但尽可能接近四舍五入：

      |GRS            x = don't care
 .1111|0xx   .1111    (no rounding)
 .1111|100            tie case is impossible
 .1111|101  1.000     (round up)
 .1111|11x  1.000     (round up)

在舍入之前，硬件计算三个额外的数字：保护位 (G)、舍入位 (R) 和粘性位 (S)，但由于平局情况是不可能的，我们只需要知道 G。 因此，在任何格式中，精确结果的小数部分具有 $r$ 位，然后要舍入到下一个整数，则要求小数部分至少具有 $r+1$ 前导位。 我声称这在法律投入下是不可能的。

由于我们只需要考虑小数部分会发生什么，让我们将 $x/y$ 的确切结果分解为整数 $n$ 和小数部分：

\[\frac{x}{y} = n + \frac{a}{b}\]

（其中 $b=y$ 只是为了不那么碍眼）很明显：

\[\frac{a}{b} \in \left[0,1\right)\]

给定 $p$ 精度二进制浮点格式，除法生成 $d$ 位整数，留下 $r$ 位作为余数：

\[\begin{align*} d & = \left \lfloor \log_2 \left(n \right)+1 \right \rfloor \\ r & = p-d \\ \end{align*}\]

对于 $r$ 位小数部分，我们可以定义 $b$ 值范围的下限和上限：

\[\begin{align*} \func{b_l}{r} & = 2^r \\ \func{b_u}{r} & = 2^{r+1}-1 \end{align*}\]

至此，我们已经基本完成了 $p$、$n$ 及其派生的 $d$。 我们想知道 $r$ 位可能的最大小数部分。

我们可以用较低的值创建最接近 $1$ 的值是：

\[\begin{align*} \frac{2^r-1}{2^r} = \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{1}{2^i} \end{align*}\]

重写为总和告诉我们这是在二进制扩展中产生 $r$ 前导的最小数字。

现在重复上限最接近 $1$ 的值，并与 $r+1$ 领先的最小数字（$r+1$ 的下限）进行比较：

\[\begin{align*} \frac{2^{r+1}-2}{2^{r+1}-1} &< \frac{2^{r+1}-1}{2^{r+1}-0} \end{align*}\]

其中负零用于对齐表达式并突出显示模式。 无论如何，这种不等式意味着上限仅限于 $r$ 领先。

我们实际上可以具体说明边界的二进制扩展。 较低的是 $r$ 并终止。 上层的精确值是纯循环的，周期为 $r+1$，其中 $r$ 1 后跟一个零。 这是前四项的表格：

$r$ lower 二进制展开 upper 二进制展开
1 $\frac{1}{2}$ .1 $\frac{2}{3} $ .(10)
2 $\frac{3}{4}$ .11 $\frac{6}{7} $ .(110)
3 $\frac{7}{8}$ .111 $\frac{14}{15}$ .(1110)
4 $\frac{15}{16}$ .1111 $\frac{30}{31}$ .(11110)

但无论如何重要的部分是：

让我们通过考虑一些除数来简单地将这些部分联系在一起。

除以：

  • $1$ 是正确的
  • $2$ 仅修改指数并且不会发生任何类型的舍入。
  • $3$ 即 $r=1$，最大的 x % 3 值为 $2$，因此最大分数为 $\frac{2}{3}$。 无法舍入到下一个整数。
  • $\set{4,5,6,7}$有$r=2$。 确切的除数并不重要，因为它们都以 0.110x 开头。

等等所有可能的约数。
